lead: A ventilator pushes a breath into the lungs and lets it out. It is used when a patient cannot breathe enough, in the ICU, operation theatre or ambulance. Positive-pressure ventilators blow gas in; negative-pressure ventilators, such as the iron lung, lower pressure around the chest so air is sucked in. Every breath has three events: trigger, limit and cycle. The variable that ends inspiration often appears in the mode name, but not always. Pressure control is time-cycled and is named for its pressure limit, not its cycle. This idea sorts most ventilator vocabulary.
prereq: You need spirometry, lung volumes and the intra-alveolar and thoracic pressures from respiratory measurement, because ventilator pressures act across the same lung mechanics.

blocks.text: Negative-pressure ventilators lower the pressure around the chest. The iron lung is the classic example: the patient lies in a chamber, chamber pressure falls, and air enters the lungs because thoracic pressure is now higher than chamber pressure. Positive-pressure ventilators do the opposite: they push gas into the airway through an endotracheal tube, tracheostomy or tight-fitting mask. Invasive ventilation uses a tube; non-invasive ventilation uses a mask. Every positive-pressure breath has three separate events. The trigger starts inspiration; it can be a set time, a drop in airway pressure, or a measured patient flow. The limit caps inspiration; it can be a set flow or a set pressure. The cycle ends inspiration; it can be volume, pressure, time, flow or the patient. The trigger, limit and cycle need not use the same variable. In pressure-control mode the limit is pressure, but the cycle is usually time. A fourth variable, the baseline, sets the pressure or flow to which the patient exhales; PEEP is a raised baseline.

Five cycling variables are named in syllabi. A volume-cycled breath ends after a set tidal volume; the ventilator measures volume and stops inspiration, so pressure rises if compliance falls. A pressure-cycled breath ends when airway pressure reaches a set value; the volume delivered then depends on compliance and resistance, so it can fall if the lung stiffens. A time-cycled breath ends after a set inspiratory time; infant ventilators often use this. A flow-cycled breath ends when inspiratory flow falls to a set fraction of its peak; pressure support uses this, because flow slows as the lung fills. A patient-cycled breath ends when the patient exhales or a demand valve closes; CPAP uses this. The figure places these five under one question.

Modes combine trigger, limit, cycle and settings. Continuous mandatory ventilation (CMV) gives set breaths at a set rate; the patient cannot trigger extra breaths. Assist-control gives the set rate, but a patient trigger also receives the full set tidal volume. Synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV) gives set mandatory breaths and allows spontaneous breaths between them; pressure support can assist those spontaneous breaths. Pressure support is patient-triggered, pressure-limited and flow-cycled. Pressure control is time-cycled and pressure-limited. Volume control is volume-cycled. CPAP is continuous positive airway pressure; the patient breathes spontaneously against a constant pressure. PEEP is positive end-expiratory pressure; it keeps small airways and alveoli open at end expiration and can be added to any mode. Settings: tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight (PBW); PBW is from height, not scale weight. Respiratory rate is breaths per minute. FiO₂ is the fraction of inspired oxygen, from 0.21 in room air to 1.0. I:E ratio is inspiratory time divided by expiratory time, often 1:2 to 1:3. PEEP is often started at 5 cm H₂O. Alarm limits watch high pressure, low volume and apnea. Dry gas needs a humidifier; see humidifiers, nebulizers and inhalers.

figure.caption: Two breaths of the worked example: constant flow of 0.375 L/s for 1.33 s delivers 500 mL, pressure climbs from PEEP 5 to a peak of 28 cmH₂O, the pause shows the plateau of 20, and passive expiration fills the remaining 2.67 s. Compliance is 500 ÷ (20 − 5) = 33.3 mL/cmH₂O and resistance (28 − 20) ÷ 0.375 = 21.3 cmH₂O per L/s.

spec.aria: Pressure-time and flow-time waveforms of two ventilator breaths: square inspiratory flow of 0.375 litres per second for 1.33 seconds, pressure rising from 5 to a 28 peak with a 20 plateau, then exponential expiratory flow back to zero over 2.67 seconds, with compliance and resistance boxes.

examples.question: A male patient is 175 cm tall. Find the tidal volume range at 6–8 mL/kg of predicted body weight. PBW = 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) for men and 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) for women; use the male formula here.
steps: Low tidal volume = 6 mL/kg × 70.6 kg = 423.6 mL; round to 424 mL.
High tidal volume = 8 mL/kg × 70.6 kg = 564.8 mL; round to 565 mL.
examples.answer: Set tidal volume between about 424 mL and 565 mL.
examples.check:
h = 175
pbw_exact = 50 + 0.91 * (h - 152.4)
pbw = round(pbw_exact, 1)
low = round(pbw * 6)
high = round(pbw * 8)
print(pbw)
print(low)
print(high)

examples.question: A volume-controlled ventilator is set to a rate of 15 breaths/min, an I:E ratio of 1:2, a tidal volume of 500 mL with constant inspiratory flow, and PEEP 5 cmH₂O. The monitor shows a peak pressure of 28 cmH₂O and a plateau pressure of 20 cmH₂O. Find the inspiratory and expiratory times, the minute ventilation, the inspiratory flow, the static compliance and the airway resistance.
steps: I:E = 1:2 splits it into 3 parts: T<sub>i</sub> = 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33 s and T<sub>e</sub> = 2 × 4 ÷ 3 = 2.67 s.
Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate = 0.5 L × 15 = 7.5 L/min.
Inspiratory flow = 0.5 L ÷ 1.33 s = 0.375 L/s = 22.5 L/min.
Static compliance = V<sub>t</sub> ÷ (plateau − PEEP) = 500 mL ÷ (20 − 5) cmH₂O = 33.3 mL/cmH₂O, lower than the 50–100 of a healthy ventilated adult, so the lungs are stiff.
Airway resistance = (peak − plateau) ÷ flow = (28 − 20) ÷ 0.375 = 21.3 cmH₂O per L/s, about twice the usual value for an adult tube, so look for secretions or a kinked or narrow tube.
examples.answer: T<sub>i</sub> = 1.33 s, T<sub>e</sub> = 2.67 s, minute ventilation 7.5 L/min, flow 0.375 L/s (22.5 L/min), compliance 33.3 mL/cmH₂O and resistance 21.3 cmH₂O per L/s.

traps: Pressure control is usually time-cycled, not pressure-cycled; the name comes from the pressure limit.
Use predicted body weight from height for tidal volume, not the weight on the weighing scale.
CPAP is not a full mandatory breath; the patient does the work while pressure stays positive.
PEEP is end-expiratory pressure, not peak inspiratory pressure; a high peak pressure alarm is different.
Pressure-cycled ventilation gives a variable tidal volume when lung compliance changes; volume-cycled ventilation keeps volume but pressure may rise.

quiz.q: Define trigger, limit and cycle of a ventilator breath.
quiz.a: Trigger starts inspiration; limit caps it; cycle ends it.

quiz.q: Why is pressure control usually time-cycled rather than pressure-cycled?
quiz.a: Pressure rises to the set level within a fraction of the breath, so cycling on pressure would end inspiration almost at once and give an uncontrolled, variable inspiratory time. Setting a time keeps inspiratory time, I:E ratio and mean airway pressure predictable, and the pressure limit still caps the pressure.

quiz.q: A 160 cm male patient needs tidal volume at 6 mL/kg PBW. Compute PBW and tidal volume.
A patient on volume control has peak pressure rising. What does that suggest?
quiz.a: Volume is fixed, so rising peak pressure means higher airway resistance or lower compliance. Check plateau pressure: high peak pressure with normal plateau means raised resistance (secretions, bronchospasm, tube biting); high plateau as well means low compliance (pneumothorax, consolidation, abdominal distension).

quiz.q: Which mode is patient-triggered, pressure-limited and flow-cycled?
State the difference between SIMV and assist-control.
quiz.a: Assist-control gives a full set breath for every patient trigger. SIMV gives set mandatory breaths and lets spontaneous breaths occur between them, often with pressure support.

quiz.q: Why set tidal volume on predicted body weight, not actual weight?
quiz.a: Lung size follows height, not fat mass. Using actual weight in obese patients overdistends alveoli and can cause lung injury.

beyond: Not for the exam. ICU ventilators now offer closed-loop modes such as adaptive support ventilation, which adjust pressure support to the patient's effort. Research studies driving pressure and low tidal volume to reduce ventilator-induced lung injury. Search for 'lung-protective ventilation', 'driving pressure', 'APRV' and 'non-invasive ventilation'.
